screens.title: SUDO and Privilege Escalation Management

In this lesson you will learn how sudo provides controlled, auditable privilege escalation so individual users can perform specific administrative tasks without sharing the root password. By the end of the chapter you will be able to write least-privilege sudoers entries, test them, and set up logging to detect misuse. To start, note three core topics you will explore: safe editing with visudo, composing secure sudoers rules, and auditing sudo activity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives set clear milestones for working with sudo in production. First, you will understand why sudo is preferred for delegated administrative tasks: it enables per-user control and records who ran what, which supports the principle of least privilege. Second, you will master editing the sudoers file safely with visudo so you never accidentally lock out administrative access. Third, you will implement granular sudo policies using aliases, runas restrictions, and careful NOPASSWD use to automate tasks without compromising security. Fourth, you will configure sudo logging so that command execution and, when necessary, command input and output can be captured for auditing and incident response. Each objective is paired with a small skill: writing an entry that allows a user to run only specific commands, testing an entry with sudo -l, creating Cmnd_Alias groups for maintainability, and enabling Defaults logfile plus log_input and log_output for detailed records. These objectives are practical: you will apply them to user roles such as service accounts, web admins, and full administrators, and you will be able to explain trade-offs and common mistakes when reviewing sudoers entries.

Practice & Validation

Backup

Create a copy of /etc/sudoers before editing so you can restore if necessary.

Edit

Quick Tip

screens.title: Why use sudo? Principle of least privilege and auditable actions
screens.narratorSegment: Sudo is designed to let permitted users run specific commands as another user while retaining an audit trail. Define sudo as a delegation tool that records who executed what and typically requires the current user's password rather than the root password. This supports the principle of least privilege: give users only the commands they need, not full root access. A concrete example is granting a web operator permission to restart a specific service without exposing the root account: you might allow a user to run /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd but no other root commands. The common misconception is that sudo is only about convenience; in fact, its logging and runas features make it a security control. Another confusion is thinking sudo replaces the need for careful command paths — it does not. Always use absolute paths in sudoers entries to avoid PATH-based hijacking. In practice, adopt a policy of minimal command lists, prefer aliases for groups of related tasks, and audit changes frequently. A practical takeaway: treat sudoers edits like changes to access control — back them up, test them, and ensure they are minimal. How might you reduce risk when a user must automate tasks? Consider narrowly scoped NOPASSWD entries only for those exact commands.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Why use sudo?
Definition

Sudo allows specified users to run commands as another user, usually root, while recording who ran the command and requiring the invoking user's password.

Concrete example
# Allow ops to restart httpd only
webop ALL=(root) /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd
Common misconception

Sudo is not just convenience: its authentication and logging are security features. Also, sudo does not protect against poorly specified command paths; use absolute paths.

Key Takeaway

Grant only the commands a user needs and ensure those entries are testable and logged.

Visual: Delegation cards
User
webop
Authentication with webop's password, not root's.
Command
/usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd
Absolute path prevents PATH hijacking.
Audit
Sudo records which user ran the command and when, enabling forensics if something goes wrong.

screens.title: Editing /etc/sudoers safely with visudo
screens.narratorSegment: Editing /etc/sudoers directly is dangerous because a single syntax error can remove administrative access. Visudo wraps the editor with a syntax checker so you cannot save invalid entries. Start by running sudo visudo; this opens the system's configured editor and will validate syntax on save. If visudo finds an error it refuses to save and signals the problem, letting you correct it. A concrete example: add a test line for a demo user, then save and run sudo -l -U demo to confirm. Common mistakes include using an unfamiliar editor without knowing how to save and exit, or making multiple changes without testing each one. Always create a backup first with sudo cp /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers. bak so you can restore if needed. When automating changes in configuration management, use visudo's -c mode to check syntax non-interactively before deployment. Final takeaway: treat sudoers edits like any critical access change — backup, validate, test, and roll back if necessary. What will you do first before editing sudoers on a production server? Editing /etc/sudoers safely with visudo means use sudo visudo to edit sudoers safely; backup first and validate changes with sudo -l and visudo -c.. In practical terms, why visudo is mandatory and how it protects administrative access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › visudo
Steps to edit safely
  1. Backup: sudo cp /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.bak
  2. Edit: sudo visudo and make changes within the editor.
  3. Validate: visudo will check syntax on save; use visudo -c to check files non-interactively.
  4. Test: sudo -l -U username and run allowed commands to confirm behavior.
Warning

Do not edit /etc/sudoers with a plain text editor; a syntax mistake can lock out all admin access.

Quick command examples
# Backup
sudo cp /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.bak

# Edit safely
sudo visudo

# Non-interactive check
sudo visudo -c

# List allowed commands for a user
sudo -l -U alice
Example scenario

You add a single line for a test user, save via visudo, then run sudo -l for that user. If visudo reports an error, it will prompt you to fix or abort without saving.

Common mistake

Forgetting to use absolute paths or inserting uncontrolled wildcards can open broader privileges than intended. Always specify full command paths in your sudoers entries.

screens.title: Sudoers syntax — user, host, runas, and command fields
screens.narratorSegment: The /etc/sudoers file uses a clear structure to declare who can run what, from where, and as whom. A typical entry looks like: user_name ALL=(ALL) ALL. Break that down: the user specification names the user or %group; the host specification restricts the rule to particular hosts or ALL; the runas specification in parentheses sets which user or group the command runs as, defaulting to root; and the command specification lists absolute-path commands, Cmnd_Alias names, or ALL. A concrete example from the chapter: alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL — this is very permissive and risky, because it allows alice to run any command without a password. A safer construction is to use Cmnd_Alias for a group of commands and then reference that alias, which makes the file easier to read and reduces mistakes. Common misconceptions include thinking that leaving off runas implies the invoking user becomes root without restriction — always be explicit when you need a specific runas user. Practical tip: include comments above complex entries explaining intent, and always test lines with sudo -l and as the target user when possible.

keyIdea.title: Sudoers anatomy
keyIdea.text: Each sudoers line encodes user, host, runas, and command; prefer aliases and absolute paths to reduce complexity and risk.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Sudoers Syntax
Row format
user_spec  host_spec=(runas_spec)  tag_list:  command_spec

# Example
user_name  ALL=(ALL)  ALL
Elements: user or %group, host constraint, runas user or group, optional tags like NOPASSWD, and the allowed commands. Use absolute paths for commands.
Example: safer use
Cmnd_Alias WEB_SERVICES = /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd, /usr/sbin/systemctl status httpd
WEBADMINS ALL=(root) WEB_SERVICES
This grants only two commands to the WEBADMINS alias, improving readability and limiting scope.
Runas specifics

Runas allows specifying a user and optionally a group using (user:group). When omitted, commands run as root by default. For database maintenance, you may want commands to run as the postgres user.

Misconception check

Never assume an entry applied system-wide. If the host field restricts a rule to a hostname, it will not apply elsewhere. Use host specifications intentionally.

screens.title: Aliases in sudoers — User_Alias and Cmnd_Alias
screens.narratorSegment: Aliases make complex sudoers files readable and maintainable by grouping users, hosts, runas targets, and commands under single labels. Define User_Alias to list accounts, and Cmnd_Alias to list exact commands. A practical example from the chapter is User_Alias WEBADMINS = john, jane and Cmnd_Alias WEB_SERVICES = /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd, /usr/sbin/systemctl status httpd followed by WEBADMINS ALL=(root) WEB_SERVICES. This pattern keeps rules short and reduces human error when updates are needed. A common mistake is creating overly broad aliases that inadvertently expand privileges; aliases must be curated and audited like any access control list. Also avoid mixing aliases and partial wildcards in ways that obscure what a user can actually run. In larger environments, aliases support role-based administration, letting you map teams to sets of commands rather than editing dozens of per-user lines. The takeaway: use aliases to implement least privilege cleanly, and review them regularly so they stay aligned with team responsibilities. In practical terms, group users and commands for maintainability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Aliases
Alias examples
User_Alias      WEBADMINS = john, jane
Cmnd_Alias      WEB_SERVICES = /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd, /usr/sbin/systemctl status httpd
WEBADMINS ALL=(root) WEB_SERVICES
Aliases let you change membership or command lists in one place instead of editing many lines. They help when teams or responsibilities change.
Operational tip

When adding or removing users from an alias, prefer group membership for dynamic team changes instead of editing sudoers directly. Still use visudo for edits.

Misuse example

An alias that expands to ALL or includes wildcards can unintentionally grant broad root access. Audit aliases for overly permissive entries.

screens.title: NOPASSWD and tag usage — benefits and risks
screens.narratorSegment: NOPASSWD is a sudoers tag that lets a user run specified commands without entering their password. This can be useful for automation or frequent tasks where password prompts would interrupt scripts. For example, adminuser ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd allows that user to restart the httpd service without a password. However, NOPASSWD weakens the authentication barrier and should never be used with ALL or broad command lists. A common security risk is granting NOPASSWD: ALL to a user or group, which effectively bypasses sudo's authentication and makes privilege escalation trivial if the user's account is compromised. When you need automation, prefer creating a narrowly scoped NOPASSWD rule for exact commands or use a dedicated service account with constrained privileges. Always document NOPASSWD entries, restrict them to necessary hosts, and pair them with strict logging. The practical takeaway: NOPASSWD has valid uses, but treat it like an exception, not a default. Ask: can the automation use a dedicated service account instead? NOPASSWD and tag usage — benefits and risks means use nopasswd sparingly for specific automation tasks; never apply it to all or broad command sets.. In practical terms, when to allow passwordless commands and when to avoid it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › NOPASSWD
Example: narrow NOPASSWD
adminuser ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd

This is acceptable for automation that only needs to restart a specific service. Use exact paths and exact commands.

Danger: broad NOPASSWD
%dev_team ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
This configuration removes the authentication barrier and is a major security risk. Avoid it in production.
Mitigation

If automation requires passwordless execution, use a dedicated service account with a Cmnd_Alias for precisely the commands it needs, and enable strict logging for that account.

screens.title: Sudo logging and auditing
screens.narratorSegment: Logging sudo activity is essential for auditing and incident response. By default, sudo records actions to /var/log/secure on RHEL/CentOS or /var/log/auth. log on Debian/Ubuntu, but you can configure a dedicated log with Defaults logfile=/var/log/sudo. log. For higher fidelity, Defaults log_input and Defaults log_output record command input and output, helping reconstruct what was run during a privileged session. A concrete configuration set from the chapter is to add Defaults logfile=/var/log/sudo. log, Defaults log_input, and Defaults log_output to the top of /etc/sudoers via visudo. After enabling logging, test by running a sample privileged command and tailing the log to confirm entries are written. A common misconception is thinking logging alone prevents misuse; it doesn't stop attacks but provides a record for detection and post-incident analysis. Balance logging with privacy and storage considerations; enable input/output capture only for systems where it is operationally required and where storage and retention are planned. The key step: enable logging, verify entries, and ensure log rotation and access controls for the log file. Sudo logging and auditing means configure a dedicated sudo logfile and enable input/output logging for critical systems, then verify and rotate logs securely.. In practical terms, configure defaults logfile, log_input, and log_output for forensic records. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: su vs sudo — differences and recommended practice
screens.narratorSegment: Su and sudo both enable privilege escalation, but they do so differently and serve different operational needs. Su switches the current user to another account, commonly root, and requires the target user's password. Su - provides a full login environment for the target user. Because su relies on the target password and does not attribute each command to the original user, it is less auditable. Sudo, on the other hand, executes individual commands as another user, typically requiring the invoking user's password and recording who ran the command. Best practice is to prefer sudo for day-to-day administrative tasks because it preserves accountability and supports least privilege. Su is appropriate in specific scenarios, such as when you need a full root environment for a complex sequence of commands or when sudo is not configured, but use it sparingly and ensure proper auditing around sessions. A practical variation is using sudo -i or sudo su - when a login shell is required; these commands remain auditable because the initial action is recorded by sudo. Closing question: when you need to perform a multi-step maintenance window, how will you preserve auditability while using a root shell?

screens.title: Common sudoers mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: System administrators commonly make avoidable mistakes when configuring sudo. One major error is editing /etc/sudoers without visudo, which can introduce syntax errors that lock out all administrators. Another frequent problem is specifying commands without absolute paths; that leaves sudo entries vulnerable to PATH hijacking where a malicious executable earlier in PATH could run instead. Wildcards in command specifications can expand permissions unexpectedly — for example, allowing /usr/bin/* could permit many unwanted actions. Overly permissive NOPASSWD entries or group entries that grant ALL are also dangerous and remove the authentication barrier. Finally, stale sudoers entries for inactive users lead to unnecessary risk. To avoid these mistakes, always use visudo, prefer explicit absolute paths, use Cmnd_Alias for clarity, avoid broad wildcards, periodically audit sudoers for inactive users, and configure logging to detect misuse. A practical workflow: backup, edit in visudo, use sudo -l to test, and check the configured sudo log for evidence of correct behavior. The question to reflect on: when was your last sudoers review and what cleanup would you schedule today? fullNarratorScript:
In multi-user Linux systems, giving everyone root access is risky and hard to audit. In this lesson you will learn how sudo provides controlled, auditable privilege escalation so individual users can perform specific administrative tasks without sharing the root password. We will emphasize the safety pattern of using visudo to edit the /etc/sudoers file, how to craft granular entries with aliases and runas restrictions, and why logging is essential. You will see concrete examples like granting a user the ability to restart a service, creating a Cmnd_Alias for web maintenance, and configuring sudo to log input and output for forensic analysis. We will also contrast sudo with su so you know when each tool is appropriate, and show common mistakes such as editing sudoers with a regular editor or using NOPASSWD: ALL without care. By the end of the chapter you will be able to write least-privilege sudoers entries, test them, and set up logging to detect misuse. To start, note three core topics you will explore: safe editing with visudo, composing secure sudoers rules, and auditing sudo activity.

These learning objectives set clear milestones for working with sudo in production. First, you will understand why sudo is preferred for delegated administrative tasks: it enables per-user control and records who ran what, which supports the principle of least privilege. Second, you will master editing the sudoers file safely with visudo so you never accidentally lock out administrative access. Third, you will implement granular sudo policies using aliases, runas restrictions, and careful NOPASSWD use to automate tasks without compromising security. Fourth, you will configure sudo logging so that command execution and, when necessary, command input and output can be captured for auditing and incident response. Each objective is paired with a small skill: writing an entry that allows a user to run only specific commands, testing an entry with sudo -l, creating Cmnd_Alias groups for maintainability, and enabling Defaults logfile plus log_input and log_output for detailed records. These objectives are practical: you will apply them to user roles such as service accounts, web admins, and full administrators, and you will be able to explain trade-offs and common mistakes when reviewing sudoers entries.

Beyond knowing concepts you must verify them. This screen focuses on practical validation steps you should be able to perform. You will back up /etc/sudoers before making changes, edit the file using visudo so syntax is checked, and then use sudo -l to list allowed commands for a target user. For access checks, you will also use sudo -u to run a command as another user, confirming runas behavior. In a lab scenario, you'll configure three accounts: one with demonstration full access, one with restricted service permissions, and a service account with NOPASSWD for a very narrow automation task. You'll test password prompts and view the configured sudo log to ensure entries are recorded. Skill checks include composing a db_admin sudoers line that restricts execution to pg_dump and pg_restore from a single host, and explaining the risks of granting NOPASSWD: ALL. These validation tasks ensure you don't just write entries, you confirm they behave as intended and generate audit data for incident response.

Sudo is designed to let permitted users run specific commands as another user while retaining an audit trail. Define sudo as a delegation tool that records who executed what and typically requires the current user's password rather than the root password. This supports the principle of least privilege: give users only the commands they need, not full root access. A concrete example is granting a web operator permission to restart a specific service without exposing the root account: you might allow a user to run /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd but no other root commands. The common misconception is that sudo is only about convenience; in fact, its logging and runas features make it a security control. Another confusion is thinking sudo replaces the need for careful command paths — it does not. Always use absolute paths in sudoers entries to avoid PATH-based hijacking. In practice, adopt a policy of minimal command lists, prefer aliases for groups of related tasks, and audit changes frequently. A practical takeaway: treat sudoers edits like changes to access control — back them up, test them, and ensure they are minimal. How might you reduce risk when a user must automate tasks? Consider narrowly scoped NOPASSWD entries only for those exact commands.

Editing /etc/sudoers directly is dangerous because a single syntax error can remove administrative access. Visudo wraps the editor with a syntax checker so you cannot save invalid entries. Start by running sudo visudo; this opens the system's configured editor and will validate syntax on save. If visudo finds an error it refuses to save and signals the problem, letting you correct it. A concrete example: add a test line for a demo user, then save and run sudo -l -U demo to confirm. Common mistakes include using an unfamiliar editor without knowing how to save and exit, or making multiple changes without testing each one. Always create a backup first with sudo cp /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers. bak so you can restore if needed. When automating changes in configuration management, use visudo's -c mode to check syntax non-interactively before deployment. Final takeaway: treat sudoers edits like any critical access change — backup, validate, test, and roll back if necessary. What will you do first before editing sudoers on a production server? Editing /etc/sudoers safely with visudo means use sudo visudo to edit sudoers safely; backup first and validate changes with sudo -l and visudo -c.. In practical terms, why visudo is mandatory and how it protects administrative access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The /etc/sudoers file uses a clear structure to declare who can run what, from where, and as whom. A typical entry looks like: user_name ALL=(ALL) ALL. Break that down: the user specification names the user or %group; the host specification restricts the rule to particular hosts or ALL; the runas specification in parentheses sets which user or group the command runs as, defaulting to root; and the command specification lists absolute-path commands, Cmnd_Alias names, or ALL. A concrete example from the chapter: alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL — this is very permissive and risky, because it allows alice to run any command without a password. A safer construction is to use Cmnd_Alias for a group of commands and then reference that alias, which makes the file easier to read and reduces mistakes. Common misconceptions include thinking that leaving off runas implies the invoking user becomes root without restriction — always be explicit when you need a specific runas user. Practical tip: include comments above complex entries explaining intent, and always test lines with sudo -l and as the target user when possible.

Aliases make complex sudoers files readable and maintainable by grouping users, hosts, runas targets, and commands under single labels. Define User_Alias to list accounts, and Cmnd_Alias to list exact commands. A practical example from the chapter is User_Alias WEBADMINS = john, jane and Cmnd_Alias WEB_SERVICES = /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd, /usr/sbin/systemctl status httpd followed by WEBADMINS ALL=(root) WEB_SERVICES. This pattern keeps rules short and reduces human error when updates are needed. A common mistake is creating overly broad aliases that inadvertently expand privileges; aliases must be curated and audited like any access control list. Also avoid mixing aliases and partial wildcards in ways that obscure what a user can actually run. In larger environments, aliases support role-based administration, letting you map teams to sets of commands rather than editing dozens of per-user lines. The takeaway: use aliases to implement least privilege cleanly, and review them regularly so they stay aligned with team responsibilities. Aliases in sudoers — User_Alias and Cmnd_Alias means aliases improve clarity and reduce duplication; use cmnd_alias and user_alias to express roles and prepare for audits.. In practical terms, group users and commands for maintainability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NOPASSWD is a sudoers tag that lets a user run specified commands without entering their password. This can be useful for automation or frequent tasks where password prompts would interrupt scripts. For example, adminuser ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/systemctl restart httpd allows that user to restart the httpd service without a password. However, NOPASSWD weakens the authentication barrier and should never be used with ALL or broad command lists. A common security risk is granting NOPASSWD: ALL to a user or group, which effectively bypasses sudo's authentication and makes privilege escalation trivial if the user's account is compromised. When you need automation, prefer creating a narrowly scoped NOPASSWD rule for exact commands or use a dedicated service account with constrained privileges. Always document NOPASSWD entries, restrict them to necessary hosts, and pair them with strict logging. The practical takeaway: NOPASSWD has valid uses, but treat it like an exception, not a default. Ask: can the automation use a dedicated service account instead? NOPASSWD and tag usage — benefits and risks means use nopasswd sparingly for specific automation tasks; never apply it to all or broad command sets.. In practical terms, when to allow passwordless commands and when to avoid it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logging sudo activity is essential for auditing and incident response. By default, sudo records actions to /var/log/secure on RHEL/CentOS or /var/log/auth. log on Debian/Ubuntu, but you can configure a dedicated log with Defaults logfile=/var/log/sudo. log. Su and sudo both enable privilege escalation, but they do so differently and serve different operational needs. Su switches the current user to another account, commonly root, and requires the target user's password. Su - provides a full login environment for the target user. Because su relies on the target password and does not attribute each command to the original user, it is less auditable. Sudo, on the other hand, executes individual commands as another user, typically requiring the invoking user's password and recording who ran the command. Best practice is to prefer sudo for day-to-day administrative tasks because it preserves accountability and supports least privilege. Su is appropriate in specific scenarios, such as when you need a full root environment for a complex sequence of commands or when sudo is not configured, but use it sparingly and ensure proper auditing around sessions. A practical variation is using sudo -i or sudo su - when a login shell is required; these commands remain auditable because the initial action is recorded by sudo. System administrators commonly make avoidable mistakes when configuring sudo. One major error is editing /etc/sudoers without visudo, which can introduce syntax errors that lock out all administrators. Another frequent problem is specifying commands without absolute paths; that leaves sudo entries vulnerable to PATH hijacking where a malicious executable earlier in PATH could run instead. Wildcards in command specifications can expand permissions unexpectedly — for example, allowing /usr/bin/* could permit many unwanted actions. Overly permissive NOPASSWD entries or group entries that grant ALL are also dangerous and remove the authentication barrier. Finally, stale sudoers entries for inactive users lead to unnecessary risk. To avoid these mistakes, always use visudo, prefer explicit absolute paths, use Cmnd_Alias for clarity, avoid broad wildcards, periodically audit sudoers for inactive users, and configure logging to detect misuse. A practical workflow: backup, edit in visudo, use sudo -l to test, and check the configured sudo log for evidence of correct behavior. Here are the essential concepts to keep in mind. Sudo is the mechanism for delegated, auditable command execution and enforces least privilege when entries are narrowly written. The /etc/sudoers file is the authoritative configuration, and you must edit it with visudo to prevent syntax mistakes that could remove administrative access. NOPASSWD lets a user run specified commands without a password and is useful for automation, but when applied broadly it undermines authentication and should be avoided except in tightly scoped cases. These three ideas form the foundation of secure sudo usage: delegate minimally, edit safely, and restrict passwordless execution to exact commands.
